edges.effect_quant: Across large observational datasets, habitual coffee intake is associated with a meaningfully lower incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma, with stronger protection at higher intake levels.
edges.population: general adults, including people with chronic liver disease risk
edges.mechanism: Coffee delivers chlorogenic acids, diterpenes, and other compounds that may reduce hepatic inflammation, improve insulin sensitivity, and dampen fibrogenic signaling. The signal fits liver biology more than a generic healthy-user effect because the inverse association persists across hepatitis, alcohol, and metabolic-risk strata in multiple cohort analyses.
edges.summary: The most persuasive evidence comes from dose-response meta-analyses of cohort-heavy observational data rather than any single study. Those reviews consistently find lower hepatocellular carcinoma risk among coffee drinkers, with the clearest reductions appearing when intake reaches roughly two or more cups per day.
edges.caveats: This is observational evidence, so residual confounding remains possible. People with advanced liver disease may also change coffee habits over time, which can complicate reverse-causality handling in some cohorts.

evidence.citation: Bravi F et al 2013 Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol
evidence.notes: Coffee reduces risk for hepatocellular carcinoma: an updated meta-analysis.
